_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies". A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn. "cue" is when the talk comes on: "start" as the lesson opens, {"after": "<figure>"} once that figure's task is done, or "check" as the final check opens. "locals" names who in town asked a forecast question, by the forecast's "id" in the lesson file.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla. The harvest is in and you still have a job. In August I said you were trained. I may have exaggerated a little.

replies.back: One lesson’s worth. Autumn is here, and the Pacific is lining up storms like boxcars on a siding.
Suspicious, as ever. Good. Autumn is here, and the Pacific is lining up storms like boxcars on a siding.

turns.them: Ole wants to drill his winter wheat just ahead of a good rain, and he wants you to say when. Hap is flying the mail to Spokane twice this week. And Edna Pruitt has a bazaar on the green on Saturday. Outdoors. With pies.

replies.back: The Ladies’ Aid runs on pie. So does this county.

replies.say: That’s a lot of people counting on me.
replies.back: That’s what a forecaster is. You get used to it, or you take up farming.

turns.them: This week you put it all together: barometer, wind, and every cloud from the first cirrus to the last shower. By Saturday you should read a storm two days off.

replies.back: There’s a good one at the post office. Tap the glass gently. Mr. Ames does not like it tapped hard.

turns.them: You’ve watched a whole one go by. When does the barometer stop falling and start to climb?

replies.back: The squall goes through, the wind swings northwest, and up she goes. Tap the glass and you’ll see it jump.
No, it’s still falling then. It bottoms out at the cold front and climbs behind it.
It steadies there, but it doesn’t climb until the cold front has gone by.

turns.them: Hap wants to know the worst hour to be up in it.

replies.say: Under the cold front’s squall line.
replies.back: Gusts, towers, maybe hail. Tell him to sit that hour out in the hangar with a coffee.
Low and wet, but smooth. It’s the cold front’s line of towers that bites. Tell him to sit that hour out.

turns.them: That’s our lot, living on the dry side. Seattle gets the soaking and we get the leftovers. So how does the air come down to us off the mountains?

replies.say: Warmer and drier, warming at the dry rate.
replies.back: With no cloud left to slow it. That’s why your rain gauge is so lonely.

replies.say: Colder, after the snow on the passes.
replies.back: It’s cold at the crest, but it warms all the way down, at the dry rate. It reaches us warmer and drier.

replies.say: Just as moist as it started.
replies.back: It left its water on the western slopes. It comes down warmer and drier.

turns.them: Which gives Edna’s bazaar a fighting chance. A tent, mind. Not a promise.

replies.say: I’ll tell her the mountains are on her side.
replies.back: Tell her that and she’ll knit them a scarf.

turns.them: That’s the photographs. Now Ole, Hap and Edna. Get these right and I’ll stop calling you tenderfoot.

replies.say: What will you call me then?
replies.back: Harrow. Same as always. But I’ll mean it differently.
